title: Coroner's inquest into Abby in-custody death; Woman was 'sleeping off the effects of alcohol'
article: The BC Coroner's service has scheduled a formal inquest Oct. 26 to Oct. 29 for the in-custody death of an Abbotsford woman in 2008.

Christine Bernadette Miller, 39, was pronounced dead Aug. 8, 2008 after being rushed to Matsqui-Sumas-Abbotsford General Hospital following her arrest and incarceration in an Abbotsford Police Department holding cell on Aug. 7, 2008.

According to a spokesperson at the Ministry of Public Safety and Solicitor General, coroner Vincent Stancato will preside over the inquest with a jury present to publicly hear evidence from subpoenaed witnesses in order to determine the facts surrounding Miller's death.

Inquests for in-custody deaths were mandatory until this year when provincial legislation introduced in March amended the stipulation, allowing inquests to be performed at the discretion of the chief coroner.
Rod MacKenzie, chief legal counsel for the BC Coroners Service, said the amendment was based on making the best use of medical and legal resources.
Many in-custody deaths are the result of natural causes, such as heart attacks and old age, and cannot be prevented, he said.

"Inquests into such deaths did not result in recommendations which would enhance inmate or public safety. By giving the chief coroner discretion, the province and the legislature ensure more resources will be available," MacKenzie said.
"Those inquests are expected to produce recommendations that will improve public safety."
APD Const. Ian MacDonald said Miller's death was a tragedy, and the department is looking forward to further clarity on what could have contributed to her death.
"The coroner's inquest will be helpful for everybody involved, including our police department," he said.
"If there is an opportunity for us to be exposed to recommendations, or suggestions coming out of the inquiry, then we will be receptive to those."
Abbotsford officers were familiar with Miller, MacDonald said, and the department had contact with her about a dozen times.

"I don't know that she or her family would summarize her interactions with police as all being positive, I don't think they would portray her from a criminal code standpoint as being squeaky clean, but none of that should have much bearing on what happened on August 8, which, from everyone's acknowledgement is a tragedy," MacDonald said.
The night she died, Miller was taken into custody after police received a 911 call shortly after 6 p.m. regarding her condition.
"The person who phoned wasn't quite sure if she needed help or not, but felt that the person was intoxicated," MacDonald said.
Officers picked up Miller and transported her back to cells for her own safety and "to give her a place that she could sleep off the effects of the alcohol," MacDonald said.
"Again, that was something that happened previously with her."

Following Miller's death, MacDonald said the arresting officer - along with patrol staff - received additional training protocols for dealing with detainees suffering from the effects of drugs or alcohol.

David Eby, executive director of the B.C. Civil Liberties Association, said giving the chief coroner discretion on in-custody deaths can free up valuable resources, but the association is troubled by the decision.
"There are many times when a scenario might appear to be one thing, but it is actually another," Eby said.
He used the 1998 death of Frank Paul as an example.
Paul was a homeless, Aboriginal man who, police first claimed, was released from custody and later died after passing out and freezing to death in a Vancouver back alley.
w According to BC Coroners Service statistics, 267 people died in custody or in police-related deaths between 1992 and 2007 in British Columbia, for an average of 18 deaths a year.
Of those 267 fatalities, 23 are categorized as "Undetermined," 96 as "Other," and 77 as "Police Custody - Cell/Lockup."
The inquest takes place at the Coroners Court at 4720 Kingsway in Burnaby.
